concept.name: Volume analysis
concept.definition: The study of trading volume — the number of shares or contracts exchanged over a period — and of how that volume behaves relative to price movement, used to gauge the participation and conviction behind a move. In the Wyckoff tradition it is formalized as the effort-versus-result principle: volume is the effort, price change is the result. It is an analytical framework, not a proven predictive law.
concept.intuition: Price tells you what happened; volume tells you how much conviction was behind it. The same price move means something different on heavy participation than on a thin, uninterested tape.
concept.mechanics: Practitioners compare absolute and relative volume (against recent averages or prior comparable swings) with price spread and direction, looking for harmony (effort producing a commensurate result) or discrepancy (heavy volume with little progress, or progress on shrinking volume).
concept.failure_modes: In decentralized markets such as spot forex there is no consolidated volume, so tick or futures-proxy volume can mislead. Volume spikes from contract rollovers, expirations, or index rebalancing are structural and can be mistaken for conviction.
concept.misconceptions: High volume by itself predicts nothing about direction — it records participation, and every transaction pairs a buyer with a seller, so 'more buyers than sellers' is a category error that volume analysis carefully avoids.
concept.example: A stock breaks out of a month-long range on volume three times its 20-day average, suggesting broad participation; the identical breakout on half the average volume would be treated as suspect.
